newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Appeals Court declines to block CSX offer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Appeals Court declines to block CSX offer.

text.p: A federal appeals court panel Wednesday denied Norfolk Southern Corp.'s request for an emergency injunction blocking CSX Corp.'s tender offer for 19.9 percent of Conrail Inc.'s shares.
But the panel said it would consider Norfolk Southern's request for an expedited appeal, and asked parties in the case to submit arguments by 2 p.m. EST (7 p.m. GMT) on Thursday.

The panel's openness to an appeal raised a cloud of uncertainty over the takeover battle for Conrail, a Northeast railroad that has rejected a $10 billion offer from Norfolk Southern in favour of a $8.5 billion merger with CSX Corp.
The action came a day after a federal court in Philadelphia paved the way for the proposed Conrail-CSX merger by denying rival Norfolk Southern Corp.'s request to block the deal.

U.S. District Judge Donald Van Artsdalen on Tuesday forcefully rejected arguments by Norfolk Southern that Conrail's board violated its duties under Pennsylvania law and misled shareholders in agreeing to merge with CSX.
CSX initially offered $8.1 billion in cash and stock for Philadelpia-based Conrail, then raised the bid to $8.5 billion earlier this month.

That decision cleared the way for CSX to proceed with the first step of the merger, the tender offer for 19.9 percent of Conrail stock at $110 a share. The Richmond, Va.-based railroad and transportation company's offer was due to expire at midnight Wednesday.

While the appeals panel denied Norfolk Southern's request for an emergency order blocking the tender offer, its willingness to hear arguments about an appeal means the court battle is far from over, takeover specialists said.
"This is a tremendous uncertainty ... it's a mess," said one takeover stock trader. "CSX would be taking a big risk by closing on a tender with possible negative appeals decision hanging over it."
He said a possible solution for CSX would be to temporarily extend the tender offer.

The case is seen as a major test of Pennsylvania's corporate law, which allows company boards to consider a wide variety of "constituents," including a company's employees, suppliers, customers and surrounding communities when evaluating takeover offers.
The companies involved had no immediate comment on the ruling by the appellate panel.
